description:
Team created for the challenge SphereX and PlanetX!
You must have one of the following skills:
Coding
Graphic Design
Web development
summary:
SPHEREx Motion Explorer is a free web app for exploring real NASA SPHEREx infrared images of any spot in the sky and seeing what moves or changes. You pick a star or type a name or coordinates. The app pulls every SPHEREx exposure of that spot from NASA’s IRSA archive, aligns them on one grid and plays them as a video. From there you can browse all 102 infrared colors, subtract one visit from another, blink frames, stack them, adjust contrast and zoom, read each photo’s metadata, and overlay Gaia and WISE catalogs.

It covers every point the challenge asks for and was tested on the five reference objects. Measured from SPHEREx data alone, Epsilon Indi B moves 4.81″ a year, against 4.68″ from Gaia. A guided Planet X hunt flags dots that show up in only one visit and that no catalog knows.

This matters because SPHEREx data arrives as hundreds of separate files per spot. The app turns them into something a student can understand in a minute, on a phone.
details:
What it does. The app opens on a star picker. Five reference objects are preloaded: Barnard’s Star, Epsilon Indi B, WISE 0855−0714, RW Aurigae and R Draconis. Four short steps walk you through:

  1. Watch every SPHEREx photo of the star as a video.
  2. “Did it move?”: a second-visit-minus-first-visit image where still stars cancel and a moving star leaves a red and blue pair, plus the motion measured from SPHEREx next to Gaia’s prediction.
  3. Its colors: a strip of all 102 SPHEREx channels, a spectrum, and a short-versus-long-wavelength view.
  4. A Planet X hunt that scans the field for dots seen in only one visit and missing from Gaia and WISE.

A last “Your turn” step holds every tool: subtraction, addition, blink, stacking, contrast and stretch, field of view, per-photo metadata (date, observation ID, archive ID, wavelength) and catalog layers. Any other position can be loaded live by name or coordinates. A separate page estimates how far SPHEREx could detect a Planet X, using a reflected-light model checked against Neptune.

How it works. A small relay forwards requests to IRSA, which does not allow direct browser access, and trims each cutout from about 4 MB to 0.4 MB. In the browser, the app parses the FITS files, applies the TAN-SIP sky coordinates and the per-pixel wavelength table (both checked against astropy), and reprojects every photo onto a north-up grid. A light fit then measures position and brightness. Motion is fitted on the 3.8 to 5 µm frames, where bright stars saturate less and cold brown dwarfs are brightest. Two stars that barely move, RW Aur and R Dra, are used as null tests to show the error floor.

Results on real data.

  • Barnard’s Star: 11.09 ± 0.27″/yr (Gaia 10.39).
  • Epsilon Indi B: 4.81 ± 0.14″/yr (Gaia 4.68).
  • WISE 0855: 6.58 ± 0.66″/yr, seen only beyond 3 µm (literature 8.15).
  • R Draconis: 0.61 times as bright between visits.

Tools.

  • Python with numpy, scipy, astropy and reproject (pipeline, 15 tests).
  • HTML, CSS and JavaScript with no framework (web app).
  • Cloudflare Workers (relay) and GitHub Pages (hosting).
  • The interface was built with help from Claude (Anthropic). I reviewed the AI-assisted code line by line and rewrote large parts of it.

Creativity and impact. Most sky viewers show one image at a time. This one turns a whole year of SPHEREx visits into motion, color and a measurement, and uses the same visit-to-visit idea to hunt for a distant planet. It runs in any browser and on a phone, without an account. That makes it usable for classrooms, amateur astronomers and quick checks by researchers.

What I considered. Honest error bars, accessibility (contrast, keyboard use, English and Spanish), slow archive responses (photos appear progressively and get cached), and clear labels that the Planet X numbers come from a model and are not a detection.
dataRefs: SPHEREx Data Release 1 at NASA/IPAC IRSA
